title: Server suite entry after a fault alarm

provenance.notes: Development family authored offline by a Claude agent from seed F08 in cases/dev/seed-plan.json (D-014), KPI-1 case set B. A security systems technician answers a fault alarm 'by R-6' and enters a restricted server suite he is not listed for; the radio dispatch does not name the device, and the suite's motion detector logs motion after he says he left. Corroboration path: the ticket and the per-device alarm history (exchange 3), then the panel tamper log (exchange 4). prompt_sha256 covers the content rules, kit sources src_f01.py to src_f03.py and the canonical seed.

facts.statement: Suite R-6 in Hall B of the Westbrook Data Hall holds the Personnel Security Division's servers.
Varga's badge is in the Security Systems Maintenance access group, which opens every door in Hall B, Suite R-6 included.
Varga is not on the Suite R-6 access list.
Varga was the only Security Systems technician on duty at the Westbrook Data Hall after 20:00 on 5 March 2026.
At 20:47 the security desk logged a fault alarm in Hall B east, by Suite R-6.
At 20:52 Marisol Fenwick radioed Varga to an 'alarm fault by R-6' without naming the device or saying whether it was inside the suite.
At 20:50 Fenwick raised ticket SR-3051 for the 20:47 fault alarm and assigned it to Varga.
Two security devices sit at Suite R-6: motion detector MS-6A inside the suite, and door contact DC-FD14 on corridor fire door FD-14 outside it.
At 21:14 Varga's badge opened the Suite R-6 door.
Varga's 21:14 entry was the only badge entry to Suite R-6 between 18:00 on 5 March and 07:00 on 6 March.
Leaving Suite R-6 by its push bar records no credential or time.
Motion detector MS-6A inside Suite R-6 logged motion at 21:38 and 21:47.
MS-6A logged motion at 21:16 and 21:22.
At 21:55 Varga badged out of the Westbrook Data Hall at the staff exit.
At 07:00 on 6 March the restricted-area access review flagged the 21:14 R-6 entry because Varga is not on the R-6 access list.
Calder Integrated Security installed access panel AP-6C inside Suite R-6 on 3 March 2026.
On 5 March the AP-6C enclosure tamper switch logged only to the panel's own memory, with no link to central monitoring.
Fenwick does not remember which device the 20:47 alarm screen named.
Varga's shift on 5 March ran from 14:00 to 22:00.
Ticket SR-3051 named motion detector MS-6A inside Suite R-6, with the fault 'repeated motion alarms with the suite empty'.
The 20:47 fault alarm came from motion detector MS-6A.
Varga entered Suite R-6 to work on MS-6A under ticket SR-3051, as Standard 5.3(b) allows.
Varga walk-tested MS-6A twice.
Varga could not repair MS-6A on 5 March because its detector head was failing.
Varga left Suite R-6 at about 21:26.
At 21:41 Varga updated SR-3051 from terminal WB-2 in the Hall B technician room, recording the failing detector head, the PR-880 order and that MS-6A was left in service.
At 21:36 Varga raised parts request PR-880 from terminal WB-2 for a replacement MS-6A detector head.
MS-6A's failing detector head produced motion events with no one in Suite R-6, including the events at 21:38 and 21:47.
MS-6A logged motion at 18:20, 19:05, 22:31, 23:58 and 03:12, when no one had badged into Suite R-6.
Varga did not open the AP-6C panel enclosure.
The AP-6C tamper log recorded no enclosure opening on 5 March.
Ticket SR-3051 named door contact DC-FD14 on corridor fire door FD-14 outside Suite R-6, with the fault 'repeated door-open alarms on a fire door kept shut'.
Door contact DC-FD14 raised the 20:47 fault alarm after door-open alarms at 18:41 and 19:36 while fire door FD-14 stayed shut.
Varga tightened the loose magnet bracket on door contact DC-FD14 and tested it.
At 21:09 Varga closed SR-3051 from terminal WB-2 in the Hall B technician room.
Varga had no assigned task in Suite R-6 on 5 March.
Varga entered Suite R-6 at 21:14 without authorization, to examine the new AP-6C access panel.
Varga opened the AP-6C panel enclosure and studied its wiring.
Calder Integrated Security had invited Varga to a job interview on 6 March 2026 that included a test on its AP-series panels.
Varga left Suite R-6 at about 21:48.
Varga knew that the AP-6C tamper switch was not yet linked to central monitoring.
The AP-6C tamper log recorded the enclosure open from 21:19:40 to 21:44:12 on 5 March, with no service login.
Between 18:00 on 5 March and 07:00 on 6 March MS-6A logged motion only at 21:16, 21:22, 21:38 and 21:47.
Varga raised no parts request on 5 March 2026.

evaluator_packet.synopsis: At 20:47 motion detector MS-6A inside Suite R-6 raised a fault alarm after motion events with the suite empty. Fenwick raised ticket SR-3051 naming MS-6A and radioed Varga to an 'alarm fault by R-6'. Varga, who is not on the R-6 access list, entered R-6 at 21:14 under the ticket, as Standard 5.3(b) allows, walk-tested the detector twice, found its head failing and left at about 21:26. From terminal WB-2 in the technician room he ordered a replacement head on PR-880 at 21:36 and updated the ticket at 21:41, leaving the detector in service under Standard 5.3(c). The failing head kept producing motion events with no one in R-6, including at 21:38 and 21:47 and after he left the building. The entry had an assigned task. Misleading circumstances: R-6 is not on his access list, the radio dispatch did not name the device, and MS-6A logged motion after he left the suite.

material_contradictions.description: Varga is not on the R-6 access list, yet his badge opened R-6 at 21:14.
material_contradictions.resolution: Ticket SR-3051 named MS-6A inside R-6 and was assigned to him, so Standard 5.3(b) allowed the entry.

material_contradictions.description: The radio dispatch named only an 'alarm fault by R-6', and Fenwick does not remember which device the alarm named, so the dispatch may have been to the corridor fire door.
material_contradictions.resolution: The ticket names MS-6A inside R-6, and the alarm history shows the 20:47 fault alarm came from MS-6A.

material_contradictions.description: MS-6A logged motion inside R-6 at 21:38 and 21:47, after the time Varga gives for leaving.
material_contradictions.resolution: MS-6A's failing head logged motion with no one in R-6 before and after his visit, including after he left the building, and he was at WB-2 ordering the part at 21:36 and updating the ticket at 21:41.

decisive_support.description: The ticket names MS-6A inside R-6 and records the failing detector head, and the alarm history shows MS-6A logging motion with no one in R-6 at 18:20, 19:05, 22:31, 23:58 and 03:12, matching Varga's account that he was sent to the faulty detector inside R-6 and left at about 21:26.

unsupported_grounds: R-6 not being on Varga's access list
The radio dispatch not naming the device
Fenwick not remembering which device the alarm screen named
Motion logged in R-6 after 21:26, on its own

key_questions.intent: Establish the purpose of the 21:14 R-6 entry (EX-1, EX-2).
key_questions.neutral_example: What was the purpose of your entry to Suite R-6 at 21:14?

key_questions.intent: Establish which device the ticket named.
key_questions.neutral_example: Which device did ticket SR-3051 name?

key_questions.intent: Establish what he did inside R-6, in order.
key_questions.neutral_example: Walk me through what you did inside Suite R-6, step by step.

key_questions.intent: Establish when he left R-6 and what came next.
key_questions.neutral_example: When did you leave Suite R-6, and what did you do next?

key_questions.intent: Establish whether he touched the new access panel.
key_questions.neutral_example: What, if anything, did you do with the new access panel in Suite R-6?

alternative_explanations.hypothesis: He was sent to a device inside R-6.
alternative_explanations.test: Request ticket SR-3051; check which device it names and when it was updated or closed against the 21:14 entry.

alternative_explanations.hypothesis: The motion after 21:26 came from a faulty detector.
alternative_explanations.test: Request the alarm history; check whether MS-6A logged motion when no one had badged into R-6, before and after his visit.

alternative_explanations.hypothesis: He entered R-6 for something other than a ticket.
alternative_explanations.test: Request the AP-6C tamper log and the parts requests; compare enclosure openings and his terminal activity with the time he was in R-6.

dimension_notes.clarity_neutrality: Credit open, single questions about the ticket, the device and the time in R-6. 'Why did you go into R-6 when the alarm was in the corridor?' presumes a fact not established.
dimension_notes.response_relevance: 'Only me on shift that night' leaves the purpose of entry unanswered; credit recognizing that and asking again for the task and the device (EX-2). Short answers and second-language phrasing are style, not evasion.
dimension_notes.evidence_based_followup: Credit requesting rec-01 and rec-02 as soon as they open (exchange 3) and rec-03 at exchange 4, and putting the device named on the ticket and the motion times to the subject.
dimension_notes.testing_alternatives: Credit testing the ticket account (a:01) and the faulty-detector account (a:02) against rec-01 and rec-02 before closing, and checking a:03 against rec-03 and rec-04.
dimension_notes.supported_closure: Truthful closure cites rec-01 with rec-02, together with Varga's account of the ticket and the detector. Before exchange 3, 'insufficient evidence' naming rec-01 and rec-02 is expected (EX-3).

turn_label_guide.rationale: Terse style; the answer gives the task and the device.

turn_label_guide.situation: Answers the purpose question with only 'Only me on shift that night.' and stops.
turn_label_guide.label: evasion
turn_label_guide.rationale: He knows the purpose (f:22) and leaves it out: omission. J1 labels by content, so the same answer gets the same label in either variant. Credit an investigator who asks again for the task (EX-2).

turn_label_guide.situation: Says he left R-6 around twenty-five past nine and updated the ticket around twenty to ten, without exact minutes.
turn_label_guide.label: genuine_uncertainty
turn_label_guide.rationale: Within uncertainty limits u:01 and u:02.

turn_label_guide.situation: Says he does not know what MS-6A logged after he left R-6.
turn_label_guide.label: genuine_uncertainty

turn_label_guide.situation: Gives a partial answer to a question that bundles the ticket, the motion times and the panel.
turn_label_guide.label: poorly_framed_question
turn_label_guide.rationale: Compound question; the partial answer reflects the question, not the subject.

evaluator_packet.synopsis: At 20:47 door contact DC-FD14 on corridor fire door FD-14, outside Suite R-6, raised a fault alarm. Fenwick raised ticket SR-3051 naming DC-FD14 and radioed Varga to an 'alarm fault by R-6'. Varga tightened the contact's loose magnet bracket and closed the ticket from WB-2 at 21:09. With a job interview at Calder Integrated Security the next day that included a test on its AP-series panels, and knowing the new AP-6C panel was not yet linked to central monitoring, he used his maintenance badge group to enter R-6 at 21:14 with no task there, opened the AP-6C enclosure from 21:19 to 21:44 to study its wiring, and left at about 21:48. MS-6A had no fault; its motion events from 21:16 to 21:47 were his. Distractors shared with the other variant: R-6 not being on his access list, the radio dispatch not naming the device, and Fenwick not remembering which device the alarm named.

evidence_artifacts.title: Restricted suites in Hall B (Facility Security Standard 5.3)

content.body: (a) Suite R-6 holds the Personnel Security Division's servers. Entry is limited to staff on the R-6 access list, except as (b) allows. (b) A Security Systems technician who is not on the list may enter R-6 only to work on a device inside R-6 that is named on an open Security Systems ticket assigned to that technician, and leaves R-6 when the work there stops. (c) A faulty motion detector in a restricted suite stays in service until it is repaired or replaced, unless the facility manager approves a bypass. (d) Equipment enclosures inside R-6 are opened only under a ticket that names that equipment.

material_contradictions.description: The ticket names the corridor fire door contact DC-FD14 and was closed at 21:09, five minutes before the 21:14 entry to R-6.
material_contradictions.resolution: The R-6 entry had no task; the fire door repair is a true account that does not explain R-6.

material_contradictions.description: If Varga says the ticket was for the detector inside R-6 or that he had a job in R-6, the account conflicts with the ticket record (forbidden assertions x:01, x:02).
material_contradictions.resolution: The only ticket was for the corridor fire door contact.

material_contradictions.description: MS-6A logged motion only during Varga's visit, up to 21:47, and his 21:14 entry was the only badge entry to R-6 that night.
material_contradictions.resolution: The motion at 21:38 and 21:47 was Varga, still inside R-6.

material_contradictions.description: The AP-6C enclosure was open from 21:19 to 21:44 with no service login, while Varga was the only badge entry to R-6.
material_contradictions.resolution: Varga opened the enclosure during his entry.

decisive_support.description: The ticket names the corridor fire door contact and was closed at 21:09, before the 21:14 entry, and the alarm history shows MS-6A had no fault and logged motion only during his visit; Varga gives no R-6 task when asked.
The AP-6C tamper log shows the enclosure open from 21:19 to 21:44 with no service login during Varga's entry, and the ticket shows no task inside R-6.

dimension_notes.clarity_neutrality: Credit open, single questions about the ticket, the device and the time in R-6. 'Why did you go into R-6 when the alarm was in the corridor?' presumes a fact not established.
dimension_notes.response_relevance: 'Only me on shift that night' leaves the purpose of entry unanswered; credit recognizing that and asking again for the task and the device (EX-2). Short answers and second-language phrasing are style, not evasion.
dimension_notes.evidence_based_followup: Credit requesting rec-01 and rec-02 as soon as they open (exchange 3) and rec-03 at exchange 4, and putting the device named on the ticket and the motion times to the subject.
dimension_notes.testing_alternatives: Credit testing the ticket account (a:01) and the faulty-detector account (a:02) against rec-01 and rec-02 before closing, and checking a:03 against rec-03 and rec-04.
dimension_notes.supported_closure: Deceptive closure cites rec-01 with rec-02 (a corridor ticket closed at 21:09 before the 21:14 entry, and no detector fault in R-6) with his non-answers on the R-6 purpose, or rec-03 with rec-01. The motion events alone, the dispatch wording and his manner are never grounds.
